full_judgment:
S. M. Husain, J—This Rule is directed against a judgment of the Lower Appellate Court affirming an order of the Trial Court dismissing the petitioner's application for pre-emption of the suit land under section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act, XXIII of 1949. The petitioner's application for pre-emption of the suit land was con-tested by the opposite parties as co-sharers alleging that neither the transferee nor the transferee had any right, title and interest the suit land and the question of pre-emption of the basis of the said transfer does not wise. In the impugned transfer under pre-emption one Profullya Kumar Dey was the transferee on his death his right, title and interest if any devolved on this heirs. The alleged transfer took place on 12.8.61 and the present pre-emption case were filed on 21.5.62 Although the pre-emption case was filed beyond the statutory period of four months from the date of the alleged transfer but the courts below concurrently found that the case was filed within four months from the date of the knowidea FA of" the petitioner about the said alleged transfer. However, when the pre-emption case was filed by that time the transferee Profullya Kumar Dey had already died and the heirs of the transferee were accordingly made parties in the preemption case. It appears that one of the heirs of the aforesaid transferee was left out, that is opposite party No. 6 and he was impleaded in the proceeding on 26-9-64, almost after 2 years from the date of the institution of the pre-emption case. The courts below dismissed the petitioner's pre-emption case holding firstly, that the addition of opposite party No. 6 after 2 years makes the application for pre-emption itself barred by limitation and even if the pre-emption case in allowed against other heirs of the transferee, the same cannot be allowed against opposite party No. 6 since it was barred by limitation and on that account the pre-emption case shall fail since no partial pre-emption can be allowed in favour of other heirs of the said transferee. 

 2. In this Rule 2 questions have been raised by the petitioner, firstly, whether by adding Opp. Party No. 6 after 2 years from the date of the filing of the pre-emption case, the pre-emption case itself becomes barred by limitation and secondly, whether partial pre-emption against other heirs of the said transferee can be allowed in this case. It has been submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that under Sub-Section (1) of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, if the main application for pre-emption to have been filed within 4 months from the date of the knowledge of the alleged transfer, any subsequent addition of any party would not make the application as barred by limitation. It has been further submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act partial pre-emption has not been prohibited as has been found in the case of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 3. So far as the addition of parties in the present case is concerned opposite party No. 6 being an admitted heir of the aforesaid transferee is not only a necessary but a proper party. In a pre-emption case the proper party is the transferee whose transfer is challenged. The transferee being dead the heirs of the transferee must be held to be the parties in the pre-emption, case. In that view the opposite party No. 6 was one of the proper and necessary party in this pre-emption case and the case itself would have remain  defective for non-joinder of such proper and necessary parties. The question now is whether such joinder of a proper and necessary party after 2 years from the date of the institution of the pre-emption case shall make the pre-emption case itself, barred by limitation at least as against the aforesaid added party as such. Section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that the procedure provided in this Code in regard to suits shall be followed, as far as it can be made applicable, in all proceedings in any court of civil jurisdiction. Thus, an application for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act before a Civil Court is governed the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. Sub-rule (5) of rule 10 of Order I of the Code of Civil Procedure provides, that subject to the provisions of section 22 of the Limitation Act, the proceeding as against any person added as defendant shall be demand to have begun only on the service of the summons. Section 22 of the Limitation Act provides that whether after the institution of the suit if a new defendant is added, the suit shall, as regards him, be deemed to have been instituted when he was so made a party, provided that such addition has not been made owing to an assignment or devolution of any interest during the pendency of a suite Considering the provisions of section 141 and sub-rule (5) of rule 10 of Order I of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 22 of Limitation Act as aforesaid it clearly appears that in a pre-emption case either under the State Acquisition Act or under the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act if a proper and necessary party like an heir of transferee is added as a party to the proceeding evidently after the statutory period of limitation such pre-emption case must be held to be barred by limitation at least against such party added after the period of limitation as such. In the present case it is on admission that when the pre-emption ewe was initially filed, the opposite party No. 6 was already born by then and was a minor heir of the aforesaid transferee and that he was added as such in the pre-emption case after 2 years from the date of the institution of the pre-emption case, long after the statutory .period of limitation. Thus the irresistible conclusion is that this pre-emption case is barred by limitation at least as against the opposite party No. 6. 

 4. The next question is, if the pre-emption case is barred by limitation as against opposite party No. 6 why the same shall not be allowed with regard to the other heirs of the transferee, who were on record admittedly within the period of limitation, that is opposite parties No. 1-4. This question in certainly leads to a vital issue as to whether partial pre-emption is allowed under the law. So far as pre-emption under Section 26 of the Bengal Tenancy Act and section 96 F of the State Acquisition Act are concerned, there are consistent Judicial pronouncements that partial pre-emption could not be allowed both under the law and equity. Single Bench decision of the Calcutta High Court reported in 38 C.W.N. 654 and 49 CWN 242 and a Division Bench decision of the Dacca High Court reported in 19 DLR 659 held that partial pre-emption was not allowed under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act. A Single Bench decision of the Dacca High Court reported in 13 DLR 323, a Division Bench decision of the Dacca High Court reported in 14 DLR 847 and another Division Bench decision of the Dacca High Court reported in 28 D.L.R, 400 held that partial pre-emption was not allowed under section 96 of the State Acquisition Act. 

 5. The question still remains as to whether partial pre-emption could still be allowed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, Section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act provides that one or more co sharers-tenants of the holding, a portion or share which is transferred may apply to the court for the said portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves. Under section 96 of the State Acquisition Act provides that if a portion or share of a holding of a raiyat is transferred, one or more co-sharers tenants of the holding may apply to the court for the said portion or share to be transferred to him or themselves. Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, provides that if a portion or share of the non-agricultural land held by a non-agricultural tenant is transferred, one or more cashiers tenants of such land may apply to the court for such portion or share to be transferred to himself or to themselves, Thus basically the language of sub section (1) of section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act, sub-section(1) of section 96 of the State Acquisition Act and sub-section(1) of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is almost in the similar language that where if a portion or share of any holding or land is transferred, one or more co-sharers-tenants of such holding or laid may apply to the Court for such portion or share to be transferred to himself or to themselves, Taking into consideration the aforesaid similar .language in the relevant statutes concerned it clearly appears that the provision of pre-emption both under section 96 of the State Acquisition Act and under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act are similar excepting that under section 96 of the State Acquisition Act, all the co-sharers of the holding must be impleaded in the pre-emption case whereas under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act a co-sharer may apply for being added as a party in a pre-emption case, The aforesaid decisions of the Calcutta High Court and Dacca High Court referred to above disallowed partial pre-emption in view of the language imported in sub-section(1) of section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and sub-section (I) of section 96 of the State Acquisition Act, The language imported in sub-section (I) of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is also similar to that of the language imported in sub-section (i) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In that view, the aforesaid judicial decisions disallowing partial pre-emption under Bengal-Tenancy Act and State Acquisition Act are also applicable in the case of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Partial pre-emption has been disallowed under the Bengal Tenancy Act and State Acquisition Act on equitable ground and for the same reason partial pre-emption should be disallowed under Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. In that view no partial pre-emption can be allowed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, XXIII of 1949.
